name: Positive Christianity
summary: Positive Christianity was the Nazi label, from Point 24 of the 1920 programme, for a supraconfessional, racial-nationalist Christianity that put the nation above denomination and fought the 'Jewish-materialist spirit'. Rosenberg set it against 'negative Christianity', and scholars dispute whether it was a coherent religious system or a racial-national ideology.
scope: Positive Christianity as the sources define it: the Nazi movement's label, from Point 24 of the 1920 NSDAP programme ('the Party as such stands for a positive Christianity without binding itself confessionally to any one denomination', s1, s3), for a supraconfessional, racial-nationalist Christianity that fought the 'Jewish-materialist spirit' (s2, s4). It covers Rosenberg's contrast of 'positive' with 'negative Christianity' (s2) and the German Christian church politics the USHMM ties to it (s3). Scholars dispute whether it was a coherent religious system (Steigmann-Gall, s4) or a racial-nationalist ideology never presented as Christian (Koehne, s2). It excludes the Confessing Church, the Catholic Church and later or non-German uses of the phrase.
